messages.subject_clean: Correlation of Latent and Observed variables
messages.body_plain:
Eaindray,
In theory, yes, you can apply multigroup analysis as described in the tutorial that Terrence linked to.  However, here are some things to consider as you proceed.

1. Your sample size is not large, so keep an eye on confidence intervals and statistical power.

2. You may want to do some reading about measurement invariance to understand the issues involved in separating your hypothesis that the bus lines differ in terms of a common construct measured by a given scale across lines from the rival hypothesis that the lines differ in how the survey items function resulting non-comparable scores.

3. Just because your ad hoc scales were supported by EFA, you cannot be sure that a CFA model will fit them.  However, even if the CFA fits, you also cannot believe the p values if you used the same data for CFA as you did for the EFA.  (If you choose a hypothesis based on the data, then it is more likely to fit the data than the assumptions underlying the p values assume.)

4. It is important that you not model mean structures in making decisions about the scales, or you cannot believe the p values for your analysis of mean differences either.  (If you choose the scales to produce mean differences, then differences are again more probable than the assumptions underlying the p values assume.)

5. You may want to first test the hypothesis that the two low bus lines are the same.  If supported, you could then combine the hypotheses that the high bus line differs from both of them whereas if not supported you need to test these separately.

Good luck,
Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

Hi Everyone!

I had a quick question regarding Multigroup Comparison in Lavaan. Conceptually speaking, if I wanted to take a fully constrained model (using group.equal = c("intercepts", "regressions")) and free specific paths, would I need to place constraints on the covariances of the model as well? This is what I am working with so far:

practicemodel4<-
  '
#Regressions
 w3DISCRIM ~ c("a1","a1")*w2DISCRIM
 w3PSSM ~ c("b1","b1")*w2PSSM + a*w2DISCRIM
 w3DEPRESS ~ c("c1","c1")*w2DEPRESS + c("d1","d1")*w2PSSM
 w4DISCRIM ~ c("e1","e1")*w3DISCRIM
 w4PSSM ~ c("f1","f1")*w3PSSM + c*w3DISCRIM
 w4DEPRESS ~ c("g1","g1")*w3DEPRESS + b*w3PSSM
 w5DISCRIM ~ c("h1","h1")*w4DISCRIM
 w5PSSM ~ c("i1","i1")*w4PSSM + c("j1","j1")*w4DISCRIM
 w5DEPRESS ~ c("k1","k1")*w4DEPRESS + d*w4PSSM

 #Direct Effects
 w4DEPRESS ~ e*w2DISCRIM
 w5DEPRESS ~ f*w3DISCRIM
 direct := e + f

 #Mediations
 med1 := a*b
 med2 := c*d
 mediated := med1 + med2

 #Covariances
 w2DISCRIM ~~ w2PSSM + w2DEPRESS
 w2PSSM ~~ w2DEPRESS
 w3DISCRIM ~~ w3PSSM + w3DEPRESS
 w3PSSM ~~ w3DEPRESS
 w4DISCRIM ~~ w4PSSM + w4DEPRESS
 w4PSSM ~~ w4DEPRESS
 w5DISCRIM ~~ w5PSSM + w5DEPRESS
 w5PSSM ~~ w5DEPRESS

 #Total Effect
 total1 := med1 + e
 total2 := med2 + f'
modelcomparison2 <- lavaan::sem(practicemodel4, data=seasons.edited, missing = 'fiml', fixed.x = FALSE, group = "groupcomp")
summary(modelcomparison2,fit.measures = TRUE)

I wanted to make sure I am doing the constraining and freeing paths correctly. Any help is appreciated!
Thank you in advance!

Sincerely,
David

messages.subject_clean: Lavaan Multigroup Comparison Question
messages.body_plain:
> would I need to place constraints on the covariances of the model as well?

I can't see why that would be necessary.

>  w3PSSM ~ c("b1","b1")*w2PSSM + a*w2DISCRIM
>

> I wanted to make sure I am doing the constraining and freeing paths correctly

You are correctly constraining the w2PSSM path by providing the same label in each group.  But you still need to provide a vector of labels (1 per group) for the w2DISCRIM path.  You only provided a single label "a", which will be applied to the first group.  If you want that to be free across groups, give them different labels (e.g., c("a1","a2")*w2DISCRIM) so that you can define the indirect effect separately per group (and also define a difference parameter to test whether they are equal across groups).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
> I fail to understand why, when I specified std.ov=TRUE and std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE in the fit function, the summary's std.all and estimates are different.

If you are asking why the std.all in the first example does not match the unstandardized estimated from the second, it is because your latent variables are not all exogenous.  std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE sets the variances in Psi to 1 for identification, but those are residual variances (only coincidentally total variances when latents are exogenous, like ind60).  If you compare them instead using the ?cfa example, you will see the std.all in the first example does match the unstandardized estimated (as well as the std.all column) from the second.

But if you merely compare the std.all columns from both of your examples, they should match (they do when I run your syntax).  But I think your output does not match because the first example seems to additionally include x1 as a predictor of dem65, which changes the meaning of the other partial regression coefficients.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Thank you so much for your feedback! I took what you said and wanted to ask if the way I coded it in R makes sense for a multigroup comparison where I am comparing a fully constrained model to a model with the mediation paths being freed:

#Full Constrained Model

practicemodel4<-
  '
#Regressions
 w3DISCRIM ~ w2DISCRIM
 w3PSSM ~ w2PSSM + c(a1,a1)*w2DISCRIM
 w3DEPRESS ~ w2DEPRESS + w2PSSM
 w4DISCRIM ~ w3DISCRIM
 w4PSSM ~ w3PSSM + c(c1,c1)*w3DISCRIM
 w4DEPRESS ~ w3DEPRESS + c(b1,b1)*w3PSSM
 w5DISCRIM ~ w4DISCRIM
 w5PSSM ~ w4PSSM + w4DISCRIM
 w5DEPRESS ~ w4DEPRESS + c(d1,d1)*w4PSSM

 #Direct Effects
 w4DEPRESS ~ c(e1,e1)*w2DISCRIM
 w5DEPRESS ~ c(f1,f1)*w3DISCRIM
 direct := e1 + f1

 #Mediations
 med1 := a1*b1
 med2 := c1*d1

 mediated := med1 + med2

 #Covariances
 w2DISCRIM ~~ w2PSSM + w2DEPRESS
 w2PSSM ~~ w2DEPRESS
 w3DISCRIM ~~ w3PSSM + w3DEPRESS
 w3PSSM ~~ w3DEPRESS
 w4DISCRIM ~~ w4PSSM + w4DEPRESS
 w4PSSM ~~ w4DEPRESS
 w5DISCRIM ~~ w5PSSM + w5DEPRESS
 w5PSSM ~~ w5DEPRESS

 #Total Effect

 total1 := med1 + e1
 total2 := med2 + f1'
modelcomparison1 <- lavaan::sem(practicemodel4, data=seasons.edited, missing = 'fiml', fixed.x = FALSE, group = "groupcomp", group.equal = c("intercepts", "regressions"))
summary(modelcomparison1,fit.measures = TRUE)
anova(modelcomparison,modelcomparison1)

#Partial Constrained Model
practicemodel5<-

  '
#Regressions
 w3DISCRIM ~ c("a1","a1")*w2DISCRIM

 w3PSSM ~ c("b1","b1")*w2PSSM + c("l1","l2")*w2DISCRIM

 w3DEPRESS ~ c("c1","c1")*w2DEPRESS + c("d1","d1")*w2PSSM
 w4DISCRIM ~ c("e1","e1")*w3DISCRIM

 w4PSSM ~ c("f1","f1")*w3PSSM + c("n1","n2")*w3DISCRIM

 w5DEPRESS ~ c("k1","k1")*w4DEPRESS + c("o1","o2")*w4PSSM

 #Direct Effects
 w4DEPRESS ~ c("p1","p2")*w2DISCRIM
 w5DEPRESS ~ c("q1","q2")*w3DISCRIM
 direct := p1 + p2 + q1 + q2

 #Mediations
 med1 := l1*m1
 med2 := l2*m2
 med3 := n1*o1
 med4 := n2*o2
 mediated := med1 + med2 + med3 + med4

 #Covariances
 w2DISCRIM ~~ w2PSSM + w2DEPRESS
 w2PSSM ~~ w2DEPRESS
 w3DISCRIM ~~ w3PSSM + w3DEPRESS
 w3PSSM ~~ w3DEPRESS
 w4DISCRIM ~~ w4PSSM + w4DEPRESS
 w4PSSM ~~ w4DEPRESS
 w5DISCRIM ~~ w5PSSM + w5DEPRESS
 w5PSSM ~~ w5DEPRESS

messages.subject: Is a MIMIC model or multigroup SEM model better?
messages.subject_clean: Is a MIMIC model or multigroup SEM model better?
messages.body_plain:
I was told that a multigroup model is good because it's more customizable, and you can compare the coefficients between groups (assuming the appropriate assumptions are met). Whereas a MIMIC model is better when you have a lot of groups. Is this an accurate summary or is there something I'm missing?

I'm currently practicing with the European Social Survey (ESS), and I have a SEM model with 16 independent variables (many are dummy variables for the endogenous variables). I'm focusing on 6 countries, so 5 of these included variables are my country variables. When I practiced using just 2 countries, I was told that while MIMIC was an option, multigroup would be better. I feel more comfortable with MIMIC but don't know if there's any good justification to use it in my case (6 countries). I think it would be interesting to know how the different countries compare to one another, but I find testing for measurement invariance and scalar invariance a bit advanced for me right now. I was also told that interpreting the regression results from the lavaan output, assuming the country dummy variables are used in the MIMIC model, is that the coefficient is relative to the reference variable (country).

If you have any insight as model types, I would really appreciate your input! Thank you.

messages.subject: MGCFA Scalar Invariance DF only change by 1. Why?
messages.subject_clean: MGCFA Scalar Invariance DF only change by 1. Why?
messages.body_plain:
Hello again,

I am wondering about my attempt to run MGCFA, specifically Scalar Invariance. Why do the Degrees of Freedom only change by 1 when I go from Metric to Scalar Invariance? Shouldn't they be changing by more? This leads me to wonder whether something is incorrect with my code/model.
Please see below my syntax, and then my output.
Thank you!
Silvi Goldstein

Syntax:
##MGCFA
##configural
fit2 <- cfa(Group1factor, ordered= c( "trafficr", "carr", "arrest", "money", "sch", "scwrk", "kids", "rents", "friend", "pass", "mem", "broke", "job"),
            data = data,
            group = "AIWhite")
summary(fit2, fit.measures = TRUE, std=TRUE)

##Metric first constrain
fit2.1 <- cfa(Group1factor,ordered= c("trafficr", "carr", "arrest", "money", "sch", "scwrk", "kids", "rents", "friend", "pass", "mem", "broke", "job"),
              data = data,
              group = "AIWhite",
              group.equal = c("loadings"))
summary(fit2.1, fit.measures= TRUE, std=TRUE)

##Scalar constrain
fit2.3 <- cfa(Group1factor,ordered= c("trafficr", "carr", "arrest", "money", "sch", "scwrk", "kids", "rents", "friend", "pass", "mem", "broke", "job"),
              data = data,
              group = "AIWhite",
              group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"))
summary(fit2.3, fit.measures= TRUE, std=TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Silvi—

You have declared observed variables as ordinal. Recent research (Wu & Estabrook 2016) has made the point that identification of ordinal variable models involves constraints on thresholds as well as loadings and intercepts. Different sets of constraints are required in different situations. So what is happening is that, as you impose more constraints, going from configural to metric to scalar invariance, other constraints are being relaxed. That is why your DF increase less than you expect. There should be lavaan documentation now that offers more specifics on what lavaan does by default.

--Ed Rigdon

Wu, H., & Estabrook, R. (2016). Identification of confirmatory factor analysis models of different levels of invariance for ordered categorical outcomes. Psychometrika, 81(4), 1014-1045.

Hello again,

I am wondering about my attempt to run MGCFA, specifically Scalar Invariance. Why do the Degrees of Freedom only change by 1 when I go from Metric to Scalar Invariance? Shouldn't they be changing by more? This leads me to wonder whether something is incorrect with my code/model.

Please see below my syntax, and then my output.

Thank you!

Silvi Goldstein

##MGCFA

##configural

fit2 <- cfa(Group1factor, ordered= c( "trafficr", "carr", "arrest", "money", "sch", "scwrk", "kids", "rents", "friend", "pass", "mem", "broke", "job"),

            data = data,

            group = "AIWhite")

summary(fit2, fit.measures = TRUE, std=TRUE)

              group.equal = c("loadings"))

messages.body_plain:
Dr. Rigdon,

I very much appreciate your reply and insight. Thank you for sharing the Wu & Estabrook article. If the intercepts are supposed to be constrained on each item, shouldn't the degrees of freedom increase by at least 13 (since there are 13 items)? In my case from Metric to Scalar, it decreased by 1. Perhaps this means something is incorrect with my code.....?

Thank you!
Silvi

On Fri, Apr 24, 2020 at 1:32 PM Edward Rigdon <edward...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Silvi—
>
> You have declared observed variables as ordinal. Recent research (Wu & Estabrook 2016) has made the point that identification of ordinal variable models involves constraints on thresholds as well as loadings and intercepts. Different sets of constraints are required in different situations. So what is happening is that, as you impose more constraints, going from configural to metric to scalar invariance, other constraints are being relaxed. That is why your DF increase less than you expect. There should be lavaan documentation now that offers more specifics on what lavaan does by default.
>
> --Ed Rigdon
>
>
>
> Wu, H., & Estabrook, R. (2016). Identification of confirmatory factor analysis models of different levels of invariance for ordered categorical outcomes. Psychometrika, 81(4), 1014-1045.
>
>
>
> From: lav...@googlegroups.com [mailto:lav...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of Silvi Goldstein
> Sent: Friday, April 24, 2020 1:11 PM
> To: lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com>
> Subject: MGCFA Scalar Invariance DF only change by 1. Why?
>
>
>
> Hello again,
>
>
>
> I am wondering about my attempt to run MGCFA, specifically Scalar Invariance. Why do the Degrees of Freedom only change by 1 when I go from Metric to Scalar Invariance? Shouldn't they be changing by more? This leads me to wonder whether something is incorrect with my code/model.
>
> Please see below my syntax, and then my output.
>
> Thank you!
>
> Silvi Goldstein
>
>
>

>
> ##MGCFA
>
> ##configural

>
>             data = data,
>
>             group = "AIWhite")
>
> summary(fit2, fit.measures = TRUE, std=TRUE)
>
>
>

>

messages.body_plain:
Silvi—

     As I meant to imply, lavaan is relaxing other constraints (which are no longer needed for identification) as it imposes the new constraints to achieve scalar invariance. Terrence Jorgensen has (or was working on) some didactic materials to make the fairly deep Wu and Estabrook insights a bit more clear.

     But you might learn a bit by examining the different outputs closely. Parameter estimates are changing from fixed to free while others are changing from free to fixed.

--Ed Rigdon

From: lav...@googlegroups.com [mailto:lav...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of Silvi Goldstein
Sent: Friday, April 24, 2020 1:59 PM
To: lav...@googlegroups.com
Subject: Re: MGCFA Scalar Invariance DF only change by 1. Why?

Dr. Rigdon,

I very much appreciate your reply and insight. Thank you for sharing the Wu & Estabrook article. If the intercepts are supposed to be constrained on each item, shouldn't the degrees of freedom increase by at least 13 (since there are 13 items)? In my case from Metric to Scalar, it decreased by 1. Perhaps this means something is incorrect with my code.....?

Thank you!
Silvi

On Fri, Apr 24, 2020 at 1:32 PM Edward Rigdon <edward...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Silvi—
>
> You have declared observed variables as ordinal. Recent research (Wu & Estabrook 2016) has made the point that identification of ordinal variable models involves constraints on thresholds as well as loadings and intercepts. Different sets of constraints are required in different situations. So what is happening is that, as you impose more constraints, going from configural to metric to scalar invariance, other constraints are being relaxed. That is why your DF increase less than you expect. There should be lavaan documentation now that offers more specifics on what lavaan does by default.
>
> --Ed Rigdon
>
>
>
> Wu, H., & Estabrook, R. (2016). Identification of confirmatory factor analysis models of different levels of invariance for ordered categorical outcomes. Psychometrika, 81(4), 1014-1045.
>
>

Dr. Rigdon,

Ah I see. Thank you very much for clarifying! I appreciate your responses!

Thank you,
Silvi

On Fri, Apr 24, 2020 at 2:22 PM Edward Rigdon <edward...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Silvi—
>
>      As I meant to imply, lavaan is relaxing other constraints (which are no longer needed for identification) as it imposes the new constraints to achieve scalar invariance. Terrence Jorgensen has (or was working on) some didactic materials to make the fairly deep Wu and Estabrook insights a bit more clear.
>
>      But you might learn a bit by examining the different outputs closely. Parameter estimates are changing from fixed to free while others are changing from free to fixed.
>
> --Ed Rigdon
>
>
>
> From: lav...@googlegroups.com [mailto:lav...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of Silvi Goldstein
> Sent: Friday, April 24, 2020 1:59 PM
> To: lav...@googlegroups.com
> Subject: Re: MGCFA Scalar Invariance DF only change by 1. Why?
>
>
>
> Dr. Rigdon,
>
>
>
> I very much appreciate your reply and insight. Thank you for sharing the Wu & Estabrook article. If the intercepts are supposed to be constrained on each item, shouldn't the degrees of freedom increase by at least 13 (since there are 13 items)? In my case from Metric to Scalar, it decreased by 1. Perhaps this means something is incorrect with my code.....?
>
>
>
> Thank you!
> Silvi
>
>
>
>
>
> On Fri, Apr 24, 2020 at 1:32 PM Edward Rigdon <edward...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Silvi—
> >
> > You have declared observed variables as ordinal. Recent research (Wu & Estabrook 2016) has made the point that identification of ordinal variable models involves constraints on thresholds as well as loadings and intercepts. Different sets of constraints are required in different situations. So what is happening is that, as you impose more constraints, going from configural to metric to scalar invariance, other constraints are being relaxed. That is why your DF increase less than you expect. There should be lavaan documentation now that offers more specifics on what lavaan does by default.
> >
> > --Ed Rigdon
> >
> >
> >
> > Wu, H., & Estabrook, R. (2016). Identification of confirmatory factor analysis models of different levels of invariance for ordered categorical outcomes. Psychometrika, 81(4), 1014-1045.

messages.subject: Re: Is a MIMIC model or multigroup SEM model better?
messages.subject_clean: Is a MIMIC model or multigroup SEM model better?
messages.body_plain:
Kelly,
  If it helps, here is another way to think about what Ed said.  When an loading differs between groups in a multi-group analysis, this represents an interaction between the latent variable and the group variable in determining the indicator value.  The effect of the latent variable differs between groups. In contrast, your MIMIC model only includes main effects for group membership on the latent variable, not interactions between the group variable and the latent variable.  That is like a multi-group model in which the intercepts of the latent variable can vary by group, but the loadings are constrained to equality across groups.  Adding a direct effect from group to an indicator in the MIMIC model would be like adding an individual intercept for the indicator to the multi-group model and allowing that intercept to vary across groups.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject: Re: MGCFA Scalar Invariance DF only change by 1. Why?
messages.subject_clean: MGCFA Scalar Invariance DF only change by 1. Why?
messages.body_plain:
> If the intercepts are supposed to be constrained on each item, shouldn't the degrees of freedom increase by at least 13 (since there are 13 items)? In my case from Metric to Scalar, it decreased by 1. Perhaps this means something is incorrect with my code.....?

The intercepts are already constrained to 0 (and therefore equal) by default.  You only have binary items, so you need to simultaneously constrain c("loadings","thresholds") and compare that model to the default configural model.  If you inspect your output more carefully, you will notice that your df did not increase when you (thought that you) added constraints on intercepts.  The df decreased by 1, indicating you estimated an additional parameter.  This occurred because asking lavaan to constrain intercept for you forced lavaan to assume this was a valid choice (even though they were already constrained), and that meant it proceeded with its default behavior to free the latent mean in the second group (which was your extra parameter).

If you instead constrained thresholds, that would trigger lavaan to free the latent scales (of y*) in group 2, which would no longer need to be fixed to 1 for identification.  Comparing that model to your metric-invariance model would show the same df but different fit (non-nested / nonequivalent models), verifying what I said above: you must compare the model with group.equal = c("loadings","thresholds") to the default configural model.  With binary items, you cannot separately test metric and scalar invariance; only an omnibus test of scalar invariance.  If violated, there is no way to distinguish which parameters are the source of violation (thresholds, intercepts, or loadings).

If you work with ordinal items with more than 2 categories, you could find the semTools::measEq.syntax() function helpful for writing lavaan scripts that write the appropriate constraints for you.  It doesn't bring much benefit for binary items though, since you can make do the comparison I described above.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Is a MIMIC model or multigroup SEM model better?
messages.subject_clean: Is a MIMIC model or multigroup SEM model better?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kelly,

Ed and Keith correctly described the assumptions of the standard MIMIC model (as well as the statistically equivalent restricted factor analysis [RFA] model, in which the grouping variable merely covaries with the factor rather than predicts it).  However, you can additionally test for differences in factor loadings by using a product-indicator approach to model an interaction between the latent factor and the grouping variable.  Oddly enough, the covariance between the latent interaction factor and the common factor captures information about heteroskedasticity of common factor variances across groups, so it is robust to "violating" that traditional assumption of MIMIC/RFA models.

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-018-1151-3 (simulation study)

https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-77249-3_20 (tutorial with example lavaan syntax)

Heteroskedasticity of residual variances is not captured (unless residual covariances with product-indicators are modeled, which would render this model underidentified), but my grad student has recently found that results are quite robust to violation of that assumption as well (only minor Type I error inflation in cases of severe residual heteroskedasticity).  Paper is still under review.  A limitation of the product-indicator approach for latent interactions is that it is only applicable to continuous indicators ("products" of ordinal variables make no sense).

The advantage of MIMIC/RFA over MG-CFA is that single-group models are more stable in smaller samples because they estimate fewer parameters (e.g., all parameters can differ across groups in MG-CFA, except for arbitrary identification constraints, which requires more observations).  However, with 5 dummy codes to represent 6 countries, you would have to calculate product indicators with each dummy code to define a latent interaction between each dummy code and the common factor(s).  So that model might get so large that it loses its small-sample advantage.

If you use MG-CFA, you still get the interpretation "relative to the reference country" because the latent mean is fixed to zero in the first (reference) country.  Thus, estimated latent means in other countries are merely differences from the reference country.  In the semTools package, the measEq.syntax() function could be helpful for writing lavaan syntax to test invariance using MG-CFA, since you are unfamiliar with it.  But I recommend reading as many textbooks, slides, or tutorials as you can find.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Since you only have observed variables in your model, you could fit the models with the lm() function to use the fitted() or predict() methods for those objects.  But since you have different predictors of each outcome, the estimated slopes will differ between lavaan and OLS to the degree that your predictors (of different outcomes) are correlated.  For instance, if you had the same predictors of each outcome (a saturated model), your estimates from lavaan would be the same as from OLS:

mod <- '
x1 ~ sex + ageyr
x2 ~ sex + ageyr
'
summary(sem(mod, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, meanstructure = TRUE))
summary(lm(x1 ~ sex + ageyr, data = HolzingerSwineford1939))
summary(lm(x2 ~ sex + ageyr, data = HolzingerSwineford1939))

SEM is trying to reproduce the observed covariances among all the variables in your model, so the restrictions (e.g., that a1 does not predict X2) force the algorithm to find estimates that reproduce some observed covariances (e.g., between a1 and X2) only indirectly via other parameters (covariance of a1 with a2 and slope of X2 on a2).

> Where are these output values in the fitted object?

They aren't.  lavaan is an SEM program, so the criterion for estimation is to reproduce summary statistics (means and covariance matrices) rather than casewise observations.  The model-implied predictions are still returned by the fitted() method, just as they are for (generalized) linear (mixed) model objects in other packages, but the fitted values are the summary statistics implied by the model's parameter estimates.  Pretty standard stuff you can find in SEM textbooks :-)

As the ?lavPredict help page states: "this function can not be used to ‘predict’ values of dependent variables, given the values of independent values (in the regression sense)."  However, Jarrett Byrnes has put together some convenience functions for lavaan objects that treat the many linear models within an SEM as individual linear models are treated in other modeling frameworks:  https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/sqehkG13lQY/mqW3Q9J9AQAJ
Eventually, lavPredict() will include some capability to return "y_hat" for observed variables, but there are many details to work out (e.g., what to do when there are latent predictors, what to return for observed ordinal outcomes (latent-response probabilities, or y-hat of latent responses), what to do when conditional.x=TRUE, etc.), and I do not think this is currently a high programming priority.  But your model seems very straight-forward, so I'm sure Jarrett's code will work in your case.

Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
> I understand how to calculate a classical Mediation in lavaan, but I don't have an idea, how to include the specification of the panel model above

It looks like plm() takes long-format data, so all the Y observations are in a single column, with another column containing an index for time.  In SEM, panel data are traditionally handled in wide format, like repeated-measures ANOVA (Y on each occasion is in a different column).  Thus, first-order autoregressive paths are specified by regressing Y at T2 on Y at T1, and first-order cross-lagged paths are specified by regressing Y at T2 on X at T1.  Within-time (error) covariance structure is specified by freeing covariances among variables at the same time.

Here is an article that discusses the traditional SEM approach to panel data, illustrated with path diagrams that are easily translated into any software's model syntax (including lavaan):  https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/9c0e/320b78f0d0c110cb6deb3586605a0a687e77.pdf

Hi Dr. Terrence,

Thank you for sharing the link to this forum and I appreciate your detailed responses to my questions. Yet, I am still uncertain about the "correct" way of testing MI with ordinal indicators. Based on Liu et al (2017), MI starts with configural, followed by equal loadings, equal thresholds and equal unique factor variances which parallels the steps for continuous indicators. Interestingly, they skipped equal intercepts as they are fixed to 0 for model identification (in Mplus, that's the default I believe). In contrast, Wu & Estobrook (2016) suggest that, beyond baseline/configural, testing equal thresholds before equal loadings and intercepts (in R, "equal intercepts" can be tested thanks to measEq.syntax()). I found this jarring and would appreciate if you could explain to me which way would be preferred.

Further, because of the different ways proposed in conducting MI, Liu et al (2017) did not define latent item responses using a single-indicator construct for each ordinal indicator. Instead, they merely specified the latent common factors using ordinal indicators with "para. =theta" and place constraints on loadings, thresholds, and residual variances accordingly (with the residual variances fixed to be 1 at time 1). I am guessing this is how they circumvent the issue of scale factors with theta param because in Mplus, theta cannot be used with scale factors while delta can (which is the default in Mplus, I made a typo in my previous message). However, in so doing, we can't really test "equal intercepts..." or is there a way to do so in Mplus? Thus, I am wondering whether "equal intercepts" is necessary for MI with categorical variables.

Thank you again for your time!

best,

> So you think this has something to do with this specific data? And that generally this shouldn't happen?

That is my best guess.  The configural model fits so poorly (and surprisingly, worse than the metric-invariance model) that I wonder whether the optimizer found a local solution that is way off out there compared to the solution found for the (also poorly fitting) metric model.  But I would still expect that the configural model should be able to fit perfectly to any model-implied covariance matrix from a more constrained metric-invariance model (that is what nesting means).

I tried empirically checking whether your models are identified.  The configural model passes the empirical check: Fitting that model to its own model-implied covariances results in finding the same solution (and thus fits perfectly).

cov_fit1 <- sapply(fitted(fit1), "[[", i = "cov", simplify = FALSE)
update(fit1, sample.cov = cov_fit1, se = "none")

update(fit2, sample.cov = cov_fit2, se = "none") # can't reproduce its own solution
update(fit1, sample.cov = cov_fit2, se = "none") # neither can the configural model

messages.subject_clean: MI with ordinal variables
messages.body_plain:
> is there a way to do so in Mplus? Thus, I am wondering whether "equal intercepts" is necessary for MI with categorical variables.

Yes, and Wu & Estabrook's (2016) example Mplus syntax shows you how to do this.  The intercepts are specified for the latent responses that represent each ordinal indicator.

The equality of intercepts or thresholds is equivalent for binary data.  For ordinal data with > 2 categories, a shift in intercepts is equivalent to a shift (in the opposite direction) of all thresholds simultaneously.  So it is less restrictive to first test thresholds without assuming equal intercepts, then test whether intercepts can be constrained too.

Mattan S. B.:
  Here are a few additional observations for what they are worth.

1. You appear to be analyzing correlations as if they were covariances.  This is not recommended.
2. I would recommend analyzing measurement invariance with a CFA model rather than, as you did, a structural model.
3. I would recommend using the CFA() function only for CFA models.
4. If you look at the correlation matrices, they are not what one would expect for homogeneous measures.  There is considerable heterogeneity in correlations across items on the same putative scale.  Moreover, these patterns seem to vary across groups.
5. Note the warning that your fit2 did not converge to a proper solution in group 1.

  My guess is that your measurement model is not well specified in one or both groups and that even if it were, it would not be invariant across groups.  My suggestion would be to go back a step to fitting the model separately in each group.  My guess is that your measures of the same construct are heterogeneous and do not all fit a common factor model.  Unfortunately, with so few measures, you cannot test this independently for each scale.  You may have to treat the eight observed variables as separate variables in a path analysis.  You could still test equality of structural parameters across groups.

Keith

messages.subject_clean: Simple question about specifying covariance of error terms for endogenous variables in the model
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I am writing to ask a technical question about specifying covariance of error terms using lavaan.

If I have two endogenous variables with error terms and I want to covary/correlate the two error terms, is the below a correct way to do this?

endogenous1 ~~ endogenous2

Also, the lavaan tutorial website seems to be inconsistent about whether the above specification is the covariance of the errors of two endogenous variables or whether it is the correlation of the errors of two endogenous variables. In one place on the tutorial website (Model Syntax 1 tab), these are labeled "residual (co)variances" http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/syntax2.html. In another place on the tutorial website (A SEM example tab), it refers to it as "residual correlations".

Which one is it? Is it technically the residual covariance (covariance of the errors)? Since correlations have to be between -1 and 1 and the example presented in the website has values that exceed this range [-1, 1].

Any clarification on this would help!!

Thank you very much!

messages.subject: Re: Simple question about specifying covariance of error terms for endogenous variables in the model
messages.subject_clean: Simple question about specifying covariance of error terms for endogenous variables in the model
messages.body_plain:
Timothy,
  'Correlation' has two meanings.  It can refer to an association that exists independently of how it might be represented, and it can also refer to a specific numerical representation of that association.  Covariance is a numerical representation of a correlation in the first sense that differs from a correlation in the second sense.

  Consequently, the error covariance represents the correlation in the first sense but does not represent it in the correlation metric unless both errors have unit variances.

   On way to relate such a covariance back to substantive theory is to think of it as representing one or more common causes omitted from the model.  If a common cause has effects of the same sign on both variables, then this would contribute to positive covariation between them.  If the signs of the effects differ, then this would contribute to negative covariation.

  Conversely, if you fix the covariance to zero, this implies that either (a) the causes in the model fully explain the covariance between the two outcomes or (b) the covariance matrix is not faithful to the underlying causal model and the effects of any omitted variables exactly cancel out to zero.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

Hello Keith,

Thank you very much for your thorough answer to my question.
So just to clarify, when I specify in the lavaan model, "endogenous1 ~~ endogenous2", it is technically estimating the covariance (and not the numerical correlation value) of the two error terms. However, a significant covariance of these error terms can be interpreted as there being a significant "correlation" of these error terms (conceptually). Is this a correct way to understand it?

Also, having a significant negative covariance of the error terms would mean that there is an omitted common cause between these two variables that influences one variable positively and influences another variable negatively.

Are these summary statements correct?

Thank you again for your help!

Sincerely,
Timothy Kim
